Sorted into Slytherin.Neville Longbottom: Neville is a Gryffindor; the Hat considered Hufflepuff, and he later pulls the Sword of Gryffindor from the hat.
Sorted into Slytherin.Luna Lovegood: Luna is a Ravenclaw, a house whose motto praises wit beyond measure as a treasure.
Sorted into Slytherin.Cedric Diggory: Cedric was a Hufflepuff, the house that values loyalty and fair play, not a Slytherin.
Sorted into Slytherin.Cho Chang: Cho is a Ravenclaw, the house of the clever, and she is her team's Seeker.
Sorted into Slytherin.Sirius Black: Sirius Black is a Gryffindor, which makes him the exception in the Black family of Slytherins.
Sorted into Slytherin.Remus Lupin: Lupin was a Gryffindor, one of the four Marauders, and a werewolf who later teaches Defense Against the Dark Arts.
Sorted into Slytherin.Peter Pettigrew: Pettigrew was a Gryffindor, though he betrayed the Potters to Voldemort and hid for years as Ron's pet rat.
Sorted into Slytherin.Albus Dumbledore: Dumbledore was a Gryffindor, and his name is an old word for bumblebee, which Rowling said suited his humming habit.
Sorted into Slytherin.Minerva McGonagall: McGonagall is a Gryffindor and head of that house, and she can transform into a tabby cat.
Sorted into Slytherin.Nymphadora Tonks: Nymphadora Tonks is a Hufflepuff and a Metamorphmagus who can change her appearance at will.

Nursery rhyme characters.Humpty Dumpty: The rhyme never says he's an egg; Lewis Carroll's Through the Looking-Glass (1871) made him one.
Nursery rhyme characters.Little Bo Peep: Bo-peep was an old hide-and-seek game; the rhyme about her lost sheep and tails to wag was in print by about 1805.
Nursery rhyme characters.Jack and Jill: The earliest known printing of this hill-climbing rhyme dates to around 1765, with a later verse added about vinegar and brown paper.
Nursery rhyme characters.Old King Cole: The merry old soul with a pipe, a bowl and fiddlers three may hark back to a legendary ancient British king, though nobody has proved which.
Nursery rhyme characters.Little Miss Muffet: A tuffet is a small footstool or grassy mound, and a spider frightening her off it appears in the rhyme by 1805.
Nursery rhyme characters.Georgie Porgie: Folk theories link him to a real George, such as George I or the Duke of Buckingham, but none is proven.
Nursery rhyme characters.Little Boy Blue: He sleeps under a haystack while the sheep are in the meadow and the cow's in the corn. Some link him to Cardinal Wolsey's servants, unproven.
Nursery rhyme characters.Old Mother Hubbard: Sarah Catherine Martin wrote it, published in 1805, and it sold thousands of copies; the rhyme about the dog and the bare cupboard.
Nursery rhyme characters.Simple Simon: He meets a pieman going to the fair and begs a taste but has no penny; chapbooks printed many comic verses about him.
Nursery rhyme characters.Little Jack Horner: He sat in a corner eating Christmas pie, stuck in his thumb and pulled out a plum; one folk theory ties him to a land-grabbing steward.
Nursery rhyme characters.Wee Willie Winkie: A Scottish poem by William Miller (1841), in which he runs through the town in his nightgown asking if children are in bed.
Nursery rhyme characters.Peter Piper: This tongue twister about a peck of pickled peppers was published in 1813 in Peter Piper's Practical Principles of Plain and Perfect Pronunciation.
Nursery rhyme characters.Jack Sprat: The rhyme about eating no fat and his wife eating no lean goes back to a proverb recorded in the 1600s.
Nursery rhyme characters.Doctor Foster: The man who went to Gloucester in a shower of rain and stepped in a puddle up to his middle; some say he's Edward I.
Nursery rhyme characters.Goldilocks: She's from the fairy tale of three bears, not a rhyme; Robert Southey told it in 1837 with an old woman, later a girl.
Nursery rhyme characters.Rumpelstiltskin: The Brothers Grimm gave us this name-guessing imp; he's a folk-tale villain, not a nursery rhyme figure.
Nursery rhyme characters.Hansel: Hansel appears in a Grimm tale with his sister Gretel, a story rather than a nursery rhyme.
Nursery rhyme characters.Pinocchio: Carlo Collodi's wooden puppet comes from a 1883 Italian novel, not a nursery rhyme.
Nursery rhyme characters.Peter Pan: J. M. Barrie's boy who wouldn't grow up debuted in a 1904 play, so he's a stage character, not rhyme.
Nursery rhyme characters.Tom Sawyer: Mark Twain's Tom Sawyer is a novel's hero (1876), nothing to do with Mother Goose.
Nursery rhyme characters.Rapunzel: Rapunzel is a Grimm fairy tale heroine whose name means rampion, a salad plant.
Nursery rhyme characters.Thumbelina: Hans Christian Andersen's tiny girl in a flower, a tale of 1835, not a nursery rhyme.
Nursery rhyme characters.Puss in Boots: Charles Perrault's clever cat in boots appears in a 1697 fairy tale, not a Mother Goose rhyme.
Nursery rhyme characters.Tiny Tim: Dickens's A Christmas Carol (1843) gave him the line "God bless us, every one"; he's a novel character, not a rhyme one.

Scottish writers.Robert Burns: Auld Lang Syne is sung worldwide at New Year, and Burns Suppers every 25 January feature haggis and his Address to a Haggis.
Scottish writers.Walter Scott: His Waverley novels popularized Scottish history, and Edinburgh's Scott Monument is among the largest memorials to a writer anywhere.
Scottish writers.R. L. Stevenson: He wrote Treasure Island for his stepson, and reportedly dreamed the plot of Jekyll and Hyde.
Scottish writers.Arthur Conan Doyle: Born in Edinburgh, he modeled Sherlock Holmes on his medical professor Joseph Bell.
Scottish writers.J. M. Barrie: From Kirriemuir, he gave Peter Pan's rights to Great Ormond Street Hospital.
Scottish writers.Muriel Spark: The Prime of Miss Jean Brodie, set in an Edinburgh girls' school, is her best-known novel.
Scottish writers.Irvine Welsh: Trainspotting, partly written in Scots dialect, made him the voice of Edinburgh's underside.
Scottish writers.Ian Rankin: His Inspector Rebus novels turned Edinburgh into one of crime fiction's great settings.
Scottish writers.Kenneth Grahame: Born in Edinburgh, he wrote The Wind in the Willows while working at the Bank of England.
Scottish writers.Val McDermid: From Fife, her crime novels about psychologist Tony Hill became the TV series Wire in the Blood.
Scottish writers.Alasdair Gray: Lanark (1981), his Glasgow-set fantasy, was a landmark, and he designed his own book covers and illustrations.
Scottish writers.James Joyce: Dublin-born James Joyce wrote Ulysses and spent most of his adult life abroad, but he is Irish rather than Scottish.
Scottish writers.Oscar Wilde: Oscar Wilde, born in Dublin, wrote The Importance of Being Earnest and is Irish, not Scottish.
Scottish writers.W. B. Yeats: W. B. Yeats won the 1923 Nobel Prize and was Irish, drawing on Sligo's landscape and folklore.
Scottish writers.Dylan Thomas: Dylan Thomas, who wrote Under Milk Wood, was Welsh and came from Swansea, so he doesn't fit a Scottish list.
Scottish writers.Roald Dahl: Roald Dahl was born in Cardiff, Wales, to Norwegian parents, so he counts as Welsh, not Scottish.
Scottish writers.Bram Stoker: Bram Stoker, Dracula's author, was born in Dublin and worked in London theater, so he's Irish, not Scottish.
Scottish writers.Jonathan Swift: Jonathan Swift, of Gulliver's Travels, was born in Dublin and became its cathedral's dean, so he's Irish.
Scottish writers.Charles Dickens: Charles Dickens was born in Portsmouth, England, and set most of his novels in London, so he's English.
Scottish writers.Thomas Hardy: Thomas Hardy, the Dorset-born author of Tess of the d'Urbervilles, is English, not Scottish.
Scottish writers.William Wordsworth: Born in Cockermouth in England's Lake District, Wordsworth wrote 'Daffodils', and he's English.
Scottish writers.Lewis Carroll: Lewis Carroll was born in Cheshire, England; his Alice stories were written in Oxford, so he is English, not Scottish.
Scottish writers.J. K. Rowling: Rowling lives in Edinburgh and wrote Harry Potter there, but she was born in Yate, near Bristol, England.
Scottish writers.Beatrix Potter: Born in London, she drew inspiration from family holidays in Perthshire, but she's English.

Foods made from milk.Cheese: Cheese comes from cow, goat, sheep or buffalo milk, and real Parmigiano-Reggiano must age at least 12 months.
Foods made from milk.Butter: It takes roughly 20 liters of milk to make a kilo of butter, which is why it was once precious.
Foods made from milk.Yogurt: Yogurt is milk fermented by bacteria, classically Lactobacillus bulgaricus and Streptococcus thermophilus.
Foods made from milk.Ice cream: Ice cream gets its smoothness from milk fat and whipped-in air, which can make up nearly half its volume.
Foods made from milk.Whipped cream: Whipped cream is air trapped in fat droplets; whip it too long and it separates into butter.
Foods made from milk.Kefir: Kefir is fermented with 'grains' made of bacteria and yeast, and the drink comes from the Caucasus.
Foods made from milk.Ghee: Ghee is butter simmered until the milk solids are removed, giving it a high smoke point and a long shelf life.
Foods made from milk.Sour cream: Sour cream is cream soured by lactic bacteria; its French cousin is crème fraîche.
Foods made from milk.Ricotta: Ricotta means 'recooked' in Italian, because it is made by reheating the whey left over from other cheeses.
Foods made from milk.Buttermilk: Traditional buttermilk was the tangy liquid left after churning butter; most store versions are cultured milk.
Foods made from milk.Paneer: Paneer is a fresh Indian cheese made by curdling hot milk with acid, and it holds its shape when cooked.
Foods made from milk.Milkshake: Malted milkshakes add malt powder made from barley, and the drink is a staple of American soda fountains.
Foods made from milk.Margarine: Margarine was invented in 1860s France as a butter substitute, originally from beef fat and milk; today it is mostly vegetable oil.
Foods made from milk.Mayonnaise: Mayonnaise is just egg yolk emulsified with oil and acid; despite the creamy look, there is no dairy.
Foods made from milk.Eggs: Eggs come from birds, not mammals, and are shelved near dairy in shops, which causes the mix-up.
Foods made from milk.Tofu: Tofu is made by curdling soy milk, much like cheese, yet it contains no dairy at all.
Foods made from milk.Almond milk: Almond milk is ground almonds and water; in the EU, plant drinks generally cannot legally be sold as 'milk'.
Foods made from milk.Coconut milk: Coconut milk is pressed from grated coconut flesh, a plant emulsion rather than anything from an animal.
Foods made from milk.Peanut butter: Peanut butter has no milk at all, and peanuts are legumes that ripen underground rather than true nuts.
Foods made from milk.Cream of tartar: Cream of tartar is neither cream nor dairy; it is potassium bitartrate, a crystalline by-product of winemaking.
Foods made from milk.Cocoa butter: Cocoa butter is the pale fat pressed from cacao beans, and it melts near body temperature, but it has no milk.
Foods made from milk.Egg whites: Egg whites are mostly water and protein, and whisking can foam them to many times their volume.
Foods made from milk.Oat milk: Oat milk is oats blended with water and strained; enzymes break down the starch, which makes it taste sweet.
Foods made from milk.Hummus: Hummus is Arabic for chickpeas, and the dip blends them with tahini, lemon and garlic, with no dairy needed.

Things with feathers.Peacock: The long train on a peacock isn't its tail but covert feathers, and the eyespots may sway more than 200 feathers in a display.
Things with feathers.Penguin: Penguins have a dense coat of short feathers, over a dozen per square centimeter, that traps air to keep them warm.
Things with feathers.Ostrich: The ostrich is the largest living bird, and it can run about 70 km/h, but it cannot fly.
Things with feathers.Velociraptor: Velociraptor was a feathered dinosaur, about the size of a turkey, and fossils show quill knobs on its forearm bones.
Things with feathers.Archaeopteryx: Archaeopteryx lived about 150 million years ago, with feathers like a bird and teeth and a long bony tail like a dinosaur.
Things with feathers.Quill pen: Quill pens were made from large flight feathers, often goose, and the best came from the left wing for right-handed writers.
Things with feathers.Shuttlecock: A shuttlecock has 16 goose or duck feathers, and it can fly off a pro badminton racket at over 400 km/h.
Things with feathers.Feather boa: Feather boas became fashionable in the Victorian era, and they were once made from ostrich plumes.
Things with feathers.Down pillow: Down is the fluffy under-layer of feathers that insulates birds, and it's the warmest insulation for its weight.
Things with feathers.Owl: Owl feathers have soft fringed edges that muffle sound, so owls fly almost silently when hunting.
Things with feathers.Kiwi bird: The kiwi's feathers look like shaggy fur, and its nostrils are at the tip of its long beak, unusual for birds.
Things with feathers.Duck: Duck feathers repel water because of an oil from a gland near the tail, which birds spread by preening.
Things with feathers.Bat: Bats are the only mammals capable of true flight, but their wings are skin stretched over long fingers, with no feathers.
Things with feathers.Flying squirrel: Flying squirrels glide with a skin flap between their limbs, rather than feathers, and can glide the length of a football field.
Things with feathers.Butterfly: Butterfly wings are covered in tiny scales, not feathers, and they are arranged like roof tiles.
Things with feathers.Dragonfly: Dragonfly wings are thin transparent membranes, and the insects are ancient, with relatives over 300 million years old.
Things with feathers.Sugar glider: Sugar gliders are small marsupials that glide using a furry membrane, and they have no feathers.
Things with feathers.Flying fish: Flying fish glide above the water on large pectoral fins, and they can stay airborne for up to 45 seconds.
Things with feathers.Bee: Bees are covered in branched hairs, which look fluffy but aren't feathers, and they catch pollen.
Things with feathers.Moth: Moth wings are dusted with tiny scales, which rub off like powder when touched.
Things with feathers.Platypus: The platypus is a mammal that lays eggs and has a duck-like bill, but it's covered in fur and not feathers.
Things with feathers.Kite: A kite is a light frame covered in paper or fabric, not feathers, and the bird of the same name does have them.
Things with feathers.Frisbee: A frisbee is a plastic disc, and the name probably came from the Frisbie Pie Company tins students tossed.
Things with feathers.Airplane: Airplane wings are metal or composite, and unlike bird wings they're fixed and do not flap.

Japanese vehicle brands.Toyota: Toyota began as a loom maker, Toyoda Automatic Loom Works, and is among the world's largest automakers by sales.
Japanese vehicle brands.Honda: Honda started with motorcycles after the war, and it became the world's biggest maker of engines of any kind.
Japanese vehicle brands.Nissan: Nissan once sold cars under the Datsun name, and the company is now the partner in an alliance with Renault.
Japanese vehicle brands.Mazda: Mazda is the only company to win Le Mans with a rotary engine, doing it in 1991 with the 787B.
Japanese vehicle brands.Subaru: Subaru is the Japanese name for the Pleiades star cluster, which is why its logo shows six stars.
Japanese vehicle brands.Mitsubishi: Mitsubishi means three diamonds, and its logo reflects that; the company makes everything from ships to cars.
Japanese vehicle brands.Suzuki: Suzuki began in 1909 as a loom maker, and it's a giant in small cars and motorcycles in India and Japan.
Japanese vehicle brands.Lexus: Lexus is Toyota's luxury brand, launched in 1989 to take on German rivals, and it has topped reliability surveys for years.
Japanese vehicle brands.Infiniti: Infiniti is Nissan's luxury arm, launched in 1989 in the US, and it was created to compete with Lexus and Acura.
Japanese vehicle brands.Datsun: Datsun was Nissan's export brand, retired in 1986 and then revived briefly in 2013 for emerging markets.
Japanese vehicle brands.Isuzu: Isuzu is named after the Isuzu River at Ise, and it's best known for trucks and diesel engines.
Japanese vehicle brands.Daihatsu: Daihatsu is Japan's oldest surviving car maker, founded in 1907, and it specializes in tiny kei cars; it's owned by Toyota.
Japanese vehicle brands.Yamaha: Yamaha began making pianos and organs, and its three-tuning-fork logo reflects that, and it also builds motorcycles.
Japanese vehicle brands.Kawasaki: Kawasaki builds motorcycles, and it also makes bullet trains, ships, and aircraft components.
Japanese vehicle brands.Hyundai: Hyundai is South Korean, and the name means modernity in Korean, and it's one of the largest car makers in the world.
Japanese vehicle brands.Kia: Kia is South Korean, founded in 1944 as a maker of bicycle parts, and it's now part of the Hyundai group.
Japanese vehicle brands.Daewoo: Daewoo was a South Korean conglomerate that collapsed in 1999, and its car business went to General Motors.
Japanese vehicle brands.Proton: Proton is Malaysia's national car brand, created in 1983 and now partly owned by Chinese company Geely.
Japanese vehicle brands.Tata: Tata is Indian, and the group bought Jaguar and Land Rover from Ford in 2008, so its British brands are not a mistake.
Japanese vehicle brands.Geely: Geely is Chinese, and it owns Volvo, which it bought from Ford in 2010, and holds a big stake in Proton of Malaysia.
Japanese vehicle brands.BYD: BYD is Chinese and began as a battery maker, and it has overtaken Tesla in sales of fully electric cars.
Japanese vehicle brands.SsangYong: SsangYong is Korean, and its name means two dragons; the brand focused on SUVs and was later rebranded KG Mobility.
Japanese vehicle brands.Genesis: Genesis is Hyundai's luxury brand from South Korea, launched as a separate marque in 2015.
Japanese vehicle brands.Lada: Lada is Russian, and the brand is built by AvtoVAZ, and its Niva has been in production since 1977.

Things in a typical living room.Sofa: The word sofa comes from the Arabic suffa, a raised bench, and it entered English through the Ottoman world in the 1600s.
Things in a typical living room.Coffee table: The low coffee table became popular in the 1900s with the rise of casual living rooms and is a mid-century design staple.
Things in a typical living room.TV: In the 1950s TVs became the focal point of living rooms, and the arrangement of seating around a screen replaced the fireplace.
Things in a typical living room.Armchair: Armchairs were once symbols of rank, and the king's chair in royal courts often had arms that lesser seats lacked.
Things in a typical living room.Rug: Persian rugs can take months or even years to weave by hand, and fine ones are traded as investments.
Things in a typical living room.Bookshelf: Studies of home libraries link them to children's reading and success, and some people arrange their shelves by color for looks.
Things in a typical living room.Fireplace: A fireplace was once a home's center for cooking and heat, and a chimney draws smoke up because hot air rises.
Things in a typical living room.Remote control: The first wireless TV remote, Zenith's Flash-Matic of 1955, worked with a beam of light, and sunlight sometimes triggered it by mistake.
Things in a typical living room.Cushion: Cushions were luxury items in the Middle Ages, and the Victorians loved heaping them on every sofa.
Things in a typical living room.Ottoman: The ottoman takes its name from the Ottoman Empire, and the cushioned footrest style came to Europe in the 18th century.
Things in a typical living room.Recliner: The recliner traces back to a 1928 chair made by cousins in Michigan, which became La-Z-Boy.
Things in a typical living room.Bathtub: A bathtub belongs in the bathroom, and the Romans bathed in huge public baths, so private tubs are a much later home luxury.
Things in a typical living room.Toilet: Toilets belong in the bathroom, and the modern flush toilet owes much to Alexander Cumming's 1775 S-bend patent, which blocks sewer smells.
Things in a typical living room.Oven: Ovens belong in kitchens, and the first electric ovens appeared in the late 1800s.
Things in a typical living room.Stove: Stoves cook food and live in kitchens, and cast-iron versions dominated homes until the early 20th century.
Things in a typical living room.Shower: Ancient Greeks had showers using water from tanks, though the modern one belongs in a bathroom.
Things in a typical living room.Dishwasher: Josephine Cochrane invented the first practical dishwasher in 1886 after getting frustrated with broken china, and it lives in a kitchen.
Things in a typical living room.Bunk bed: Bunk beds save space in children's rooms, and in ancient times soldiers and sailors used similar stacked bunks.
Things in a typical living room.Washing machine: Washing machines sit in utility rooms or laundry areas, and the first electric home model appeared in 1908.
Things in a typical living room.Workbench: A workbench is for tools and projects in the garage or shed, rather than for sitting around.
Things in a typical living room.Lawn mower: Edwin Budding invented the lawn mower in 1830 in England, but it lives in the garden shed.
Things in a typical living room.Bidet: Bidets are common in much of Europe and Asia, and the French name means pony, because you sit astride it.
Things in a typical living room.Fridge: Refrigerators sit in kitchens, and before them, households relied on iceboxes filled with blocks of ice.
Things in a typical living room.Towel rail: A heated towel rail warms bathrooms and keeps towels dry, so it belongs there rather than in a living room.

Things in a bedroom.Bed: Archaeologists have found 77,000-year-old plant bedding in South Africa, laid with insect-repelling leaves, among the oldest beds known.
Things in a bedroom.Pillow: The oldest known pillows come from ancient Mesopotamia and were made of stone, and Egyptian ones were carved from wood.
Things in a bedroom.Duvet: Duvet is French for down, and the quilt filled with eiderdown became a European standard; Britain called it a continental quilt.
Things in a bedroom.Wardrobe: Wardrobe once meant a room for guarding robes, and the word comes from Old French garderobe, which held clothes and chamber pots.
Things in a bedroom.Nightstand: Nightstands began as a place for a chamber pot, which explains why old ones had little cupboard doors.
Things in a bedroom.Alarm clock: Levi Hutchins built a mechanical alarm clock in 1787 that rang only at 4 a.m., because he wished to wake before dawn.
Things in a bedroom.Dresser: A dresser's name comes from the act of dressing, and earlier ones were also used to display plates in kitchens.
Things in a bedroom.Mattress: The word mattress comes from Arabic matrah, a place where something is thrown, and Arab traders spread the cushion style to Europe.
Things in a bedroom.Headboard: Headboards were once a draft shield behind sleepers in cold medieval rooms, and they have remained a decorative feature.
Things in a bedroom.Bedspread: Bedspreads are decorative covers, and Victorian ones were often crocheted or embroidered with great skill.
Things in a bedroom.Oven: An oven belongs in the kitchen, and keeping it near the bed would be a fire and heat hazard.
Things in a bedroom.Bathtub: A bathtub is a plumbing fixture for the bathroom, and the Romans favored huge public baths, with private tubs a much later luxury.
Things in a bedroom.Toilet: A toilet is usually in the bathroom, though some suites connect it to the bedroom as an en suite.
Things in a bedroom.Dishwasher: A dishwasher needs a water supply and drain, so it sits in the kitchen with the dishes.
Things in a bedroom.Stove: A stove is a kitchen appliance for cooking, and heating stoves once warmed bedrooms but are not the cooking kind.
Things in a bedroom.Kitchen sink: A kitchen sink is part of the kitchen's plumbing, and the phrase everything but the kitchen sink means almost everything.
Things in a bedroom.Lawn mower: A lawn mower is kept in a shed or garage because of its fuel and noise, and it stays out of the bedroom.
Things in a bedroom.Workbench: A workbench is for projects in a garage or workshop, and sawdust and tools don't mix with a good night's sleep.
Things in a bedroom.Bidet: Bidets sit in bathrooms in many countries, and the French word means pony.
Things in a bedroom.Freezer: A freezer keeps food cold in the kitchen, and it hums loudly enough that few people would want it by their bed.
Things in a bedroom.Shower: A shower is a bathroom fixture, and ancient Greeks already enjoyed pipe-fed showers about 2,500 years ago.
Things in a bedroom.Toaster: A toaster lives in the kitchen, and crumbs in the bed would make for an unpleasant night.
Things in a bedroom.Garden hose: A garden hose is for outdoor watering, and the first rubber hoses were developed in the 19th century.
Things in a bedroom.Barbecue: A barbecue is for outdoor cooking and comes from the Taino word barbacoa, and it doesn't belong in a bedroom.

Words hiding the word 'car'.Scarf: The 'car' hides inside scarf, a word that may come from an old French word for a purse worn round the neck, not for warmth.
Words hiding the word 'car'.Carrot: Carrots were once purple and yellow; the orange kind became standard much later, partly thanks to Dutch growers.
Words hiding the word 'car'.Cartoon: Cartoon comes from Italian "cartone", a big sheet of heavy paper used for a preliminary sketch.
Words hiding the word 'car'.Scarlet: Scarlet hides 'car' in its second to fourth letters; the colour was once costly because it was made from insects.
Words hiding the word 'car'.Vicar: Vicar comes from a Latin word for "substitute", as a vicar stands in for the church's rector or bishop.
Words hiding the word 'car'.Oscar: The Oscar statuette is 34 cm tall and weighs about 3.8 kg; its name is said to come from a remark by an Academy librarian.
Words hiding the word 'car'.Carpet: Carpet starts with "car", and early carpets were heavy cloth used to cover tables, not floors.
Words hiding the word 'car'.Scary: Scary hides 'car' in the middle, and its root 'scare' is thought to come from an old Norse word.
Words hiding the word 'car'.Cargo: Cargo comes from Spanish "cargar", meaning to load, and begins with "car".
Words hiding the word 'car'.Mascara: Mascara comes from Italian "maschera" for mask, and has "car" hidden in the middle.
Words hiding the word 'car'.Carnival: Carnival is often traced to Latin "carne vale", meaning "farewell to meat", before Lent.
Words hiding the word 'car'.Crab: Crab has C, R, A, but in the wrong order for "car"; crabs also walk sideways.
Words hiding the word 'car'.Cream: Cream has "c-r-e-a-m": "car" is not in there as the letters are separated.
Words hiding the word 'car'.Coral: Coral has letters C, R, A but with an O between them in the wrong order, so no "car".
Words hiding the word 'car'.Cork: Cork comes from the Latin word for oak bark, and there's no "car" in it.
Words hiding the word 'car'.Arc: Arc is an anagram of "car", but the letters are in the wrong order.
Words hiding the word 'car'.Acre: Acre has A, C, R in a different order; an acre was once the land a team of oxen could plough in a day.
Words hiding the word 'car'.Racer: Racer looks right but "car" doesn't appear; "rac" is "car" backwards.
Words hiding the word 'car'.Cedar: Cedar has C, A, R but separated by E and D; cedar wood has a distinctive smell that repels moths.
Words hiding the word 'car'.Crash: Crash has C and R and A together, but in the order "cra", so it doesn't hide "car".
Words hiding the word 'car'.Scrap: Scrap hides "cra", not "car"; the letters are out of order.
Words hiding the word 'car'.Cobra: Cobra has C and R and A but spread out and not in order, and it hides "bra".
Words hiding the word 'car'.Chair: Chair has C, A, R, but with H and I in between, so no word "car".
Words hiding the word 'car'.Circa: Circa is Latin for "around", and C-I-R-C-A doesn't hide "car".

Parts of a sailboat.Mast: A sailboat's mast is often the tallest thing for miles on open water, and racing yachts use carbon fiber to cut weight aloft.
Parts of a sailboat.Boom: The boom swings across the cockpit in a gybe, and an uncontrolled swing can knock a sailor overboard.
Parts of a sailboat.Jib: The jib is the triangular sail ahead of the mast, and the phrase 'cut of his jib' once meant judging a sailor by his sail.
Parts of a sailboat.Mainsail: The mainsail is the biggest driver on most sloops, and reefing it shrinks the area when the wind builds.
Parts of a sailboat.Rudder: A rudder works by redirecting water flow; even a small one can turn a large boat if it is moving.
Parts of a sailboat.Tiller: A tiller is the lever that steers the rudder, and on small boats it is simply pushed away from the direction you want to go.
Parts of a sailboat.Keel: The keel keeps a sailboat from sliding sideways and its weight stops it capsizing; some racing keels weigh several tonnes.
Parts of a sailboat.Halyard: Halyards haul sails up the mast; on a ship, the name comes from 'haul yard'.
Parts of a sailboat.Spinnaker: This big balloon-like sail is flown only downwind, where it adds a huge area of cloth for extra speed.
Parts of a sailboat.Cleat: A cleat is the horned fitting where a line is tied off, and a good sailor makes it fast with a figure-eight.
Parts of a sailboat.Winch: A winch gives a sailor the mechanical advantage to trim a sail under huge load, using a ratchet and drum.
Parts of a sailboat.Aileron: Ailerons are the hinged wing flaps that roll an aircraft, which has nothing to do with a boat's steering.
Parts of a sailboat.Fuselage: The fuselage is the main body of an aircraft; the word comes from the French for 'spindle-shaped'.
Parts of a sailboat.Hubcap: A hubcap covers the wheel hub on a car, and a flying one used to be a classic cartoon hazard.
Parts of a sailboat.Muffler: A muffler quiets a car's exhaust, and the British call it a silencer.
Parts of a sailboat.Kickstand: A kickstand props up a bike or motorcycle, but it's not found on a sailboat, which sits in water.
Parts of a sailboat.Pantograph: A pantograph is the arm on a tram or electric train that collects power from overhead wires; the same word names a drawing copier.
Parts of a sailboat.Caboose: The caboose was the crew car at the end of a freight train, and most US trains stopped using them by the 1980s.
Parts of a sailboat.Landing gear: On a Boeing 747 the landing gear has 16 wheels, but a sailboat has nothing like it.

Things in ancient Rome.Totem pole: Totem poles are carved by Indigenous peoples of the Pacific Northwest, far from Rome.
Things in ancient Rome.Castle: Castles belong to the Middle Ages, after Rome, though Romans built forts.
Things in ancient Rome.Gondola: Venetian gondolas date to the Middle Ages, long after Roman times.
Things in ancient Rome.Cathedral: Cathedrals are medieval, and the great Gothic ones took centuries to build, long after Rome's pagan temples had fallen quiet.
